en: The *Jiading Biqiu Shuodanglai Bianjing* (Sūtra on the Transformations of the Future Spoken by the Bhikṣu Jiading), translated by an unknown person and appended to the Song Records.
At that time, the Bhikṣu Jiading addressed the assembled multitude, saying: "Listen attentively to what I shall now [declare]..."
The introductory, intermediate, and concluding words are without contradiction or error, just as spoken by the Buddha.
In a future age, there will be terrible transformations that are most fearsome.
If you wish to know, I shall now tell you: there is great danger in the future;
you must diligently cultivate the practice of vigor.
Having received the grace of the Buddha, I have now attained peace and security.
"You who have left the household life should follow the Buddha's teaching.
Human lifespans will reach one hundred years, yet few will attain it while many will fall short.
In future ages, evil dharmas will flourish."
Evil bhikṣus will emerge to destroy the Buddha-dharma.
When the Dharma is about to perish, people’s resolve will be weak;
they will lack any sense of aspiration and will instead harbor jealousy.
They slandered and reviled one another, becoming greedily attached to mere words;
they devoted themselves to paper and ink, taking pride in their own eyesight as the highest attainment.
Yet, there were bhikṣus who received teachings orally from their masters and recited them by heart.
Having mastered the analysis of words and meanings,
they nevertheless treat others with contempt while expounding them for their sake.
"These two families of practitioners are now further embroiled in mutual strife.
I declare that what you have said is not out of a desire for wealth or treasures;
rather, there is a contradiction between your heart and your words."
Ignorant people do not understand the meaning of the sūtras and thus misinterpret their significance; consequently,
the speaker is led astray and the listener likewise falls into error.
Their speech is not upright, and their verses are interspersed with errors.
Having studied little, they harbor arrogance and look down upon others.
In future ages, such as these people will be.
They were exceedingly numerous;
they no longer served their teachers with humility,
and spoke to the three types of preceptors, saying, "What I say is the truth."
What you have said is false and deceptive.
These bhikṣus personally don secular clothing and practice what laypeople do.
They find no joy in secluded and tranquil places;
yet, amidst the clamor and bustle of the human world, they greedily long for it with attachment and cannot distance themselves from it.
Even though they may construct Buddhist stupas and temples within that very human realm.
They were further filled with mutual jealousy.
When bhikṣus from the four quarters came to stay there,
they would only allow them to remain after demanding a payment from the monastery’s master.
Although they may dwell within their own minds harboring resentment and displeasure,
once [the visitor] has departed, they all rejoice together;
yet, the bhikṣus dwelling within the Buddhist temple harbor mutual jealousy toward one another.
Some are jealous of wealth; some are jealous of physical appearance;
some are jealous of offerings; some are jealous of noble lineage;
and some are jealous of the sūtras and the Dharma, withholding them out of stinginess and refusing to transmit them.
Chasing after those of noble status and powerful influence,
their minds become discouraged and defeated, causing them to ruin the Buddha-dharma;
they amass wealth, slaves, and livestock.
Cultivating gardens and groves is considered the highest [practice].
Internally and externally,
one merely undergoes transformation by donning the kashaya robes and shaving the head.
Day and night he diligently attended to his official duties;
the ministers and officials within the kingdom who possessed power and influence pursued and served him as if he were their own slave.
Because the household of the donor serves the Three Honored Ones,
they dare not reduce their wives' portions or deprive their children of food and clothing;
instead, they erect Buddha-stūpas and temples, and provide monasteries, robes, and bedding for the Saṃgha, ensuring that all are fully satisfied.
Fearing further scarcity, he immediately took the famous, rare, and superior treasures from his home and placed them within the stupa.
The śramaṇas residing at the monastery pursued the high official, hoping for respectful treatment;
they then seized everything contained within the donor’s stupa and brought it to the official.
When officials and leaders covet wealth and do not investigate the root or the branch, they further fail to practice goodness;
because of such greed and envy, they die and enter hell.
As for those bhikṣus, they are greedy for fame and profit.
To falsely claim as a personal favor that which belongs to the Three Honored Ones—
due to this transgression, one dies and enters hell.
Or there may be a bhikṣu who commits various evils with his own body.
One might seek to appease others with money dedicated to the Triple Gem in order to attain liberation.
Or there may be bhikṣus and laypeople who,
out of greed for the property of the Triple Gem, forcibly incur guilt and take away as much as they can carry.
Such people as these shall all enter hell.
If one acts as a Dharma teacher, a master of the Vinaya,
or one who is proficient in the four Āgamas.
Each of them forms close friendships with powerful laypeople;
sitting upon the laypeople's couches, they engage in private and secret conversations regarding the merits and faults, the good and the bad, of other individuals.
Relying on and clinging to white-robed laypeople, they exploit their power and influence;
when displeased with someone, they seek to harm or injure them.
Furthermore, when preaching the Dharma for them, they mistake the heterodox for the orthodox and the orthodox for the heterodox.
One who acts in such a manner is called a partisan of unrighteousness in the world.
The Buddha possesses the Tripiṭaka;
yet as a teacher, he would keep it secret and withhold it from transmission, failing to instruct his disciples.
Why is this? Fearing that if his disciples were to know someone was their equal, they would treat the teacher with contempt;
for this reason, he kept it secret.
What is it called for a disciple to leave the household life?
If there is nothing to learn or know, then one has left home in vain.
This causes the disciple to eventually harbor anger and contempt.
They show no longer respect for their teachers,
their speech is shallow and coarse;
such monks as these give rise to evil conduct.
Māra and his retinue all find their opportunity and fall into the realms of evil;
they instead praise themselves, asking, "Who is equal to me?
Their minds turn toward evil and the three poisons blaze intensely.
Unable to restrain themselves,
they greedily crave offerings, gifts, and material wealth;
they do not avoid sin or merit, yet they claim to be performing good deeds.
For the sake of making offerings, they further engage in mutual strife and contention;
though outwardly wearing the dharma robes, their conduct does not accord with the precepts,
and their coming and going do not follow the teachings of the Dharma.
Shaking his head and looking at his reflection, he was obsessed with sensual desires even more than ordinary people.
He lived by selling cheap goods at high prices or lending money at exorbitant interest, striving only for profit.
As for the dharmas practiced by bhikṣus, he abandoned them and did not follow them.
Obtaining even a small profit or gain, they immediately rejoice;
yet when the community of bhikṣus assembles for seated meditation or study, they cannot endure it and avoid it from afar.
Greedily seeking wealth and profit, they travel in the four directions to seek them out, unaware of their exhaustion.
They deceive and exploit the common people without ever being satisfied.
Whenever there are stūpas, monasteries, monastic quarters, bedding, or places of abundance and luxury, they vie with one another to enter therein.
Outwardly they appear to observe the precepts, but inwardly they harbor wickedness and transgression.
People seeing him treated with such respect gradually pursue the white-robed laypeople day by day.
They serve and provide for them, and the laypeople, being delighted, in turn look upon the bhikṣu with reverence.
Passing the word from one to another, they exclaim in praise: "This bhikṣu’s conduct of the precepts is pure and refined."
Unaware that their inner nature was exclusively hypocritical,
they gathered many disciples, śrāmaṇeras, and slaves;
they sought and accumulated from all four directions without ever feeling satisfied.
He says, "I maintain the precepts," yet he acts as if his years of practice have not yet matured.
His observance of the dharma is lax and he lacks faith in the retribution of sin and merit.
His speech is fierce and aggressive, and he delights in the company of wine-drinkers.
The lewd woman associates with those who engage in such affairs;
she may enter the palaces and inner chambers of officials to seek self-aggrandizement and satisfaction,
or she may join human gatherings, taking pleasure in manual labor.
In the various ways of living, they speak of the merits and demerits of royal governance;
or they discuss the victories and defeats of military forces in combat;
or they speak of bandits and thieves; or they speak of food and drink.
Or they discuss the lustful desires of women;
day and night they discourse on worldly and heterodox matters;
and they are unwilling to draw near to wise teachers or virtuous friends.
Furthermore, he becomes intimate with butchers, wicked thieves, those addicted to wine, robbers, and those who engage in illicit trade and sexual misconduct;
drinking together and sharing their daily lives, his mind gradually becomes stained by attachment as he habituates himself to their conduct.
Some diligently attend to their household affairs, while others serve as laymen's messengers, avoiding neither distance nor nearness.
People of such a sort do not understand the True Dharma;
yet they cause them to become śramaṇas, which is called "corrupting the Dharma."
Having already been unfilial toward one's parents and elders,
if one sees a precept-keeping bhikṣu or a pure and noble brahmacārin and insults them without any heart of compassion;
They harm the lives of the multitude and plunder the wealth and treasures of others;
they covet the women of others and their mouths are fond of false speech;
their domestic life is licentious and promiscuous, showing no restraint toward superiors or inferiors.
If a pure and clean bhikṣuṇī gives rise to lustful thoughts and pursues him,
she destroys and ruins her ascetic conduct.
Such individuals as these shall, in their present life, be bound by the laws of the king and cast into prison to be punished with the fivefold poisons.
Should there be kings, ministers, or commoners who commit such evil deeds, [they shall likewise suffer].
Consequently, wind and rain will not arrive at their proper times, the five grains will not flourish,
the people will fall into poverty and distress, bandits will arise everywhere,
military conflicts will frequently erupt, and the myriad people will flee in all directions.
The five clans were dispersed and the villages became desolate.
At that time, the people of the world, distressed by the lack of food and clothing,
vied with one another to become śramaṇas in order to escape the sufferings of the world.
Having become śramaṇas, they destroy the Buddha-dharma;
they treat those above and below with contempt and gather together wicked people as companions,
their intentions and wills being in accord.
They further praised one another, saying, "So-and-so’s observance of the precepts is pure;
so-and-so practices meditative concentration.
When the people heard and saw this, they believed it to be true.
If a donor invites them to turn the scriptures and preach the Dharma,
they will instead secretly lie down naked and refuse to listen or learn;
if the offerings are distributed, they will compete and quarrel over them.
They seek offerings of clothing, bedding, food, and drink without ever feeling satisfied;
they take on many disciples but do not instruct them according to the Dharma,
nor do they admonish them with the Buddha’s true precepts.
The disciples do not understand the methods for practicing the precepts, meditative concentration, and the cultivation of the Path;
instead, their teachers make it their primary concern to gather together frequently,
engaging in worldly and unrighteous discourse as their habitual occupation.
When such persons accept offerings from others,
the merit of the donor is meager while the recipient incurs calamity.
If there is an assembly of the four classes of followers gathering to expound the sutras, [it is different].
They take no pleasure in listening to it.
If there are laypeople who come wishing to hear the sutras,
they vie with one another to welcome them and provide all their necessary requirements.
They do not lose their original intent;
yet when the prohibitive precepts are taught, they engage in mutual strife and contention,
even until midnight claiming that the assembly is exhausted.
If one speaks only of these four matters according to principle, laypeople will not grow weary;
however, when the pure precepts are being recited or the Dharma is being expounded, they do not wish to hear it.
This shall be the case for bhikṣus in the future.
Those who wish to disrupt the Dharma will compete to establish Buddhist temples and hold assemblies everywhere;
on the fifteenth day of each month, there will be those who recite the precepts.
Although they gather together, they do nothing but quarrel and dispute;
they neither recite the precepts nor expound the Dharma.
When the devas and humans see the Sangha assembled and approach with the desire to hear the Dharma, [they find it thus].
Upon merely hearing of strife, they said to one another, "We have come here relying on the Dharma, yet we instead hear of quarreling; what is there to seek here?
Feeling no joy in their hearts, they departed in sorrowful dejection.
Reflecting that before long the Buddha-dharma would be extinguished,
the devas, nāgas, spirits, yakṣas, and all the benevolent ghosts and gods were filled with shared sorrow and anxiety.
They will no longer protect the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha;
they shall cause various evil spirits to suck their blood and cause them all to suffer many diseases.
Their physical strength is diminished, their countenances are withered and haggard, and they are devoid of majesty;
all this arises from this very cause.
If a bhikṣu is ill and others do not look after him, but instead harbor fear and aversion toward him, wishing for his death—this is likewise so.
At that time, because there was no one to tend to them, the sick bhikṣus eventually passed away.
As the Buddha-dharma was about to perish, both bhikṣus and laypeople became collectively stingy and greedy;
they accumulated wealth and property, refusing to practice charity.
They obtain [their results] solely through greed.
As for the *māmadi*, they do not believe in sin or merit;
they have no sense of superior or inferior, nor do they distinguish the Three Honored Ones.
They used their wealth and property without regard for the Way;
they lived in close association with women and laypeople,
drinking wine, singing, dancing, and taking pleasure in mutual entertainment.
Ordinary people have no distinction [from them] and instead harbor mutual jealousy;
for this reason, their wealth and property decline, and their undertakings do not succeed.
These types of bhikṣus act thus because of lustful desire.
They delight in living as householders and do not find fault with it as suffering;
they take pleasure in forming firm bonds with young girls. Why is this so?
The mind of a young maiden is particularly profound and weighty;
once she has gained the heart of a man, they both cherish and cling to one another, never forgetting or abandoning each other.
Or, she may live together with a dissolute woman.
Or suppose there is a bhikṣuṇī who acts as a householder’s servant;
or a bhikṣu who does not store up leftovers but subsists solely on what he begs for his own body.
All those bhikṣus who have broken the precepts will collectively loathe him and have no desire to see him.
He addressed the donors, saying:
"This bhikṣu harbors flattery and deceit within, yet outwardly he manifests as one who observes the precepts; he is not worthy of receiving offerings."
In the present age, if there are bhikṣus who violate the precepts, everyone will collectively loathe them;
yet in a future age, when they see bhikṣus who are pure and uphold the precepts, they will instead collectively hate them.
At present, monks violate the precepts in private out of fear that others might see them.
In future ages, there may be monks who,
while upholding the precepts and practicing meditative concentration, likewise fear being seen by others.
The reason for this is that in future ages, people will loathe those who uphold the precepts.
In the world to come, there will be monks who forcibly seek profit and gain while remaining ignorant of shame; such people as these, those deluded ones of that age, will all pay them reverence.
Seeing those who uphold the precepts, they instead disparage and revile them.
All things are entirely treasures,
yet because people do not recognize this, they all vanish through transformation.
The Buddha-dharma is likewise.
For this reason, the True Dharma declines and vanishes;
because it is not reverently upheld, the Dharma is brought to total extinction.
It is like a great ship that sinks when it is heavily laden;
in future ages, there will be many bhikṣus who,
through greed and delusion regarding offerings, cause the Dharma to perish.
If there are bhikṣus who uphold the precepts and protect the Vinaya,
the Dharma shall endure for a long time;
it is like the lion king, who, though dead and lying upon the ground, [remains majestic].
Neither birds nor beasts dared to approach him.
Within ten days, worms emerged from his body and began to devour his own flesh,
destroying his physical form.
Although the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma continues to endure;
neither Brahmā, Māra, the assembly of sages,
nor any heterodox paths can destroy the Buddha-dharma.
In the future, there will be those who practice non-action who enter into the Buddha-dharma seeking to become śramaṇas;
they will destroy the Buddha-dharma and further disparage one another.
Those who study the Tripiṭaka become increasingly jealous of one another;
because of this jealousy, the Buddha-dharma will quickly perish.
To protect the Buddha-dharma, one should eliminate arrogance and cast away jealousy.
In the future, those bhikṣus who envy the Buddha-dharma will be like pigs in a latrine, unaware of their own stench;
they will be as unruly and destructive as unbridled donkeys.
Disregarding prohibitions and precepts, they drink alcohol and eat meat;
they do not observe seasonal proprieties when forming friendships;
and they may breach others' walls and houses to plunder their wealth and property.
Or, having received someone's deposit, they collude in mutual deception;
they provide false testimony for one another and endure beatings,
altering the documents and bonds so that gaining much is considered their good fortune.
If, when the Saṃgha has gathered together for some communal purpose,
those of lower seniority revile and abuse the elders,
and the elders depart in silence and dejection; [this is a case of formal accusation].
At that time, those of lower status will not observe the teachings of propriety;
they will refuse to accept as their teachers those who are capable of self-restraint.
When monks engage in such strife, the Dharma will be on the verge of extinction.
The world was thrown into turmoil, and all were unsettled.
The sovereign’s conscription and labor service knew no end,
while bandits rose up together to plunder the people's wealth, which then flowed into the king's coffers.
When a ruler acquires wealth, he only serves to further increase his enemies.
His governance collapses and ruin ensues; people kill one another without restraint.
The populace falls into poverty and suffering, while deceit and craftiness proliferate.
The world suffers from drought, and wind and rain do not come at their proper times.
Grain becomes scarce and dear; kings and merchants travel beyond borders to trade.
Though they plow the fields and sow the seeds, the harvests are meager.
Day and night they toil with hardship, yet their bodies and mouths are not bound [to virtue].
They exhaust themselves for no purpose to serve the officials, while the myriad people groan in distress; thus, they do not think of preserving their own lives.
At that time, the bhikṣus likewise plow fields and travel in the four directions to engage in trade.
The administrators, whether public or private, are no different from the common folk;
it is truly a great misery.
In a future age, there shall appear three Sons of Heaven who will bring ruin upon the world.
One is named Yen-le-na (Yakṣa),
currently residing in the Central Kingdom of the South.
There shall be a son of heaven who emerges from the land of Jin in the North.
There was a son of heaven named Jianqiu.
When the Buddha-dharma was about to perish,
these three sons of heaven emerged in the Jin dynasty.
He ravaged the lands and slaughtered the people;
he destroyed stupas and monastic gardens, treated śramaṇas with contempt, and subjected them to the five tortures.
He also led his military forces to the kingdom of India.
Having devastated the land and caused much slaughter,
the Son of Heaven of the Central Kingdom shall then raise an army once more to destroy the territory of Jin along with its ministers and subjects, restoring them to their native lands.
At that time, the śramaṇas of the Jin territory were oppressed by the authorities; some died,
while others returned to lay life.
Some traveled on foot toward India;
among them were those who reached their destination and those who did not.
There were some who were blind, deaf, lame, crippled, emaciated, aged, or sickly, and thus unable to travel;
they were executed by the authorities.
At that time, the Son of Heaven in the Central Kingdom revered the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, bestowing gifts upon all.
Whenever he saw one who had violated the precepts, he would immediately reprimand and admonish them.
At that time, there was an elder bhikṣu named Śīghra,
who was thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka and preached the Dharma for the king.
The king was greatly delighted and immediately invited the assembly of monks to the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
He convened a *pañcavārṣika* festival, inviting all the disciples of Śākyamuni residing within Jambudvīpa.
He caused them all to assemble.
At that time, there was a great assembly of hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus;
this "great assembly" occurred when the Buddha-dharma was nearing its end.
Since they would never meet again, it is called "the final assembly.
At that time, those in the assembly asked one another,
"Where are your upādhyāyas and ācāryas?"
Each replied, saying,
"Our teacher fell ill and died on the way."
Those killed by bandits,
those too exhausted or weak to proceed,
and those who say they have reached their destination.
They all wept together with grief-stricken hearts, raising their voices in loud lamentation.
At that time, on the fifteenth night,
a great and violent wind and torrential rain fell from the heavens.
Regarding the preaching of the two hundred and fifty precepts, there were those among the assembly who heard them and those who did not.
At that time, the bhikṣus began to quarrel with one another, speaking loudly and shouting.
The elder bhikṣu admonished the multitude, saying:
"Virtuous ones, since you speak with such small-minded words, you must apply the Dharma and no longer utter confused speech.
I shall explain your meaning by means of the bhikṣu-dharma.
Now, all the disciples of Śākyamuni from Jambudvīpa have gathered here."
This is the end of the assembly;
that which I have studied, I shall no longer study.
I only pray that you will listen in silence to what I say.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who was intelligent and wise, having entered deeply into meditative concentration.
He said to the multitude:
"The meditative concentrations I have entered are all fully perfected."
In this great assembly, there are hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus who wish to hear the Dharma and precepts so that they may be able to uphold and practice them;
I shall now speak of them.
"I pray that all the sons of the Śākyas will listen in silence and stillness.
Then, there was another bhikṣu named Sudāyu—translated into Chinese as Rìshàn (Sun-Good)—who, having attained arhatship, rose from his seat.
With single-minded devotion, he joined his palms in salutation at the feet of the elder and then uttered a lion’s roar:
"I wish to preach the sutra; let the assembly remain silent and not be noisy.
All that is taught within the sutra, I have studied in its entirety."
There is no error, and one shall never again doubt what the Buddha has spoken.
There was an elder disciple named Shangtou (Shang-tou).
Furthermore, being of superior status yet intent on committing evil deeds,
he rose from his seat and said to Srotāpanna,
"What do you know? You do not understand the sūtras, the Dharma, or the Vinaya."
When the Elder wished to speak, they all spoke together in competition.
At that moment, the Elder struck and killed Srotāpanna with an iron pestle;
yet Srotāpanna had already transcended birth and death.
Among them was a bhikṣu who maintained the precepts;
he rose silently and departed.
At that time, there was a yakṣa who had faith in the Buddha.
He then struck and killed the bhikṣu at the head with an iron pestle.
At that moment, the earth and heavens shook in six ways,
and from within the void there naturally arose sounds of wailing and cries of grievance.
From the four directions, moreover, there fell a rain of evil portents;
from the four directions, moreover, foul vapors filled the void, and thunder resounded from all sides.
At that time, among all classes of sentient beings—
Seeing these miraculous portents, they all confronted one another and wailed aloud with grief,
saying to each other,
"Today, the Dharma of the Buddha comes to its final end."
Above, reaching as far as the twenty-eighth heaven and the formless deities,
and including the nāgas and asuras who filled the air,
they raised their voices in great lamentation and threw themselves prostrate upon the ground.
Furthermore, there were rākṣasas who honored the Dharma and yakṣas who had seen the Buddha; they all threw their entire bodies to the ground and spoke these words:
From this day forward, the sound of the two hundred and fifty precepts will no longer be heard throughout the world;
monks will no longer practice them.
The orphaned and widowed beings of the world will very quickly lose their eyesight.
Alas, the world will not endure for long;
people will kill one another without anyone to question them,
like wild beasts.
The practice of the Dharma has already declined; the Dharma drum has already burst; the gate of the nectar of immortality has already closed.
The lives of the masters of the sūtras have already perished;
the torch of the Dharma has already been extinguished; the wheel of the Dharma has already fallen.
The twelvefold scriptures have already been dispersed and explained;
the Wheel of Dharma has already been broken, the water of Dharma has already ceased,
the ocean of Dharma has already dried up, and the mountain of Dharma has already collapsed.
In all the mountain valleys, there were no longer any bhikṣus who practiced meditation with diligence.
When the devas and benevolent spirits saw that the valleys were empty and lacked anyone to revere, they all threw themselves down in despair;
the people became blind and ignorant, with no Dharma left to practice.
At that time, the hosts of Māras were all greatly rejoiced;
they presented one another with famous garments and superior robes,
for the Buddha-dharma had already been extinguished.
"Our false dharma has now finally begun to flourish;
let us rejoice and rely upon one another," said the bhikṣu Kātyāyanīputra to his disciples.
In the future, such evil transformations as these will occur.
Since the Buddha’s Dharma continues to exist today, you should practice it with diligence.
The True Dharma of the Buddha is like a deep marsh.
Sentient beings look up to it and lack for nothing;
yet if the marshes and meadows dry up,
sentient beings will suffer from hunger and exhaustion, falling into the cycle of birth and death.
It is like a merchant who does not apply himself with diligence;
his wealth and treasures diminish daily, leaving his parents, wife, and children without means of sustenance.
His body and mind burn with anguish, yet his remorse comes too late to be of avail.
Now that the True Dharma exists, it is most fitting to practice it;
you may freely choose whichever path you prefer.
However, if you are again negligent and do not wish to exert yourself with diligence, [you will suffer].
If one departs empty-handed with no attainment,
one will instead be submerged and drowned in the three miserable realms;
then it will be too late for regret.
Now you fourfold assembly should contemplate the Buddha’s profound kindness;
serve him as a son serves his father.
You four great ones must establish a powerful resolve, firm in heart and fierce in will.
By practicing with diligent effort, one may attain liberation from suffering;
yet, if at any time the body and mind become feeble and one is overwhelmed by old age and illness, [one will not escape].
Regret will be of no avail.
At present, the land and its people have not yet reached a state of extreme depravity;
weapons of war have not yet arisen, and the people remain peaceful and secure.
"Rice and grain are currently cheap and alms are easily obtained;
by maintaining mindfulness and diligent exertion, you may avoid future regret.
When the disciples heard this teaching, they were moved.
They all prostrated themselves at the feet of the Great Sage;
their hearts were filled with terror, their bodies trembled,
and weeping bitterly, they addressed him, saying:
In a future age when the Dharma has completely vanished, what will those who behold this world think? How can they bear to see it?
Today, upon hearing of these matters, our hearts are shattered.
When people of that world encounter such evil as this,
would their bodies and minds not shatter into a hundred pieces?
At that time, the disciples suddenly began to deliberate among themselves once more.
With single-minded devotion, they prostrated themselves on the ground and addressed their teacher with one voice:
"We are filled with great terror; how may we attain the Way and escape this suffering, so as not to encounter such affliction?
The Great Seer replied:
The Way has neither distance nor nearness; if one seeks it with diligence, it will be attained.
There is no sequence of before or after.
This sutra is titled *The Essential Collection of Secret Prophecies for the Future Recorded by the Great Sage Kātyāyana*.
"You should apply yourselves with diligent vigor so as to avoid this suffering.
When the disciples heard this sutra, they wept with grief, choked back their tears, prostrated themselves, and vowed to practice accordingly.
Thus ends the *Sutra on the Transformations of the Future* spoken by the Bhikṣu Kātyāyanīputra.
